subtopic_detail: A six year old who speaks freely at home but has not spoken at school for eighteen months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a six year old girl whose teacher has asked her parents to seek help. She has not spoken a word at school since she started, although she nods, points and will write answers on a whiteboard.

At home she chatters constantly, argues with her brother and tells long stories to her grandmother. At the shops she goes silent if a stranger speaks to her and hides behind her mother. Her parents say she was a cautious toddler who took a long time to warm to new people, and her hearing was tested last year and was normal.

data_table.Examination: Sits close to her mother and does not speak during the consultation, makes brief eye contact, nods and shakes her head appropriately to questions, completes a drawing task and hands it over, no repetitive movements or unusual mannerisms, plays reciprocally with a doll offered to her, articulate speech heard on a video recorded at home showing age appropriate sentences and pretend play

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for behavioural therapy delivered with the school, using graded exposure to speaking situations
options.rationale: Selective mutism responds to behavioural treatment that uses stimulus fading and shaping to extend the child's speaking from a comfortable setting into the classroom, and it works only when the school is part of the plan. Early intervention matters because prolonged non speaking entrenches avoidance and limits academic and social participation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Commence a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her speech at school in six weeks
options.rationale: Medication is an adjunct considered when a well delivered behavioural program has not produced progress, or when the anxiety is so severe that the child cannot engage with it. Starting it before any behavioural intervention reverses the accepted order of treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Refer for a multidisciplinary autism assessment before any anxiety focused intervention is commenced
options.rationale: Autism is the differential when social communication differences persist across all settings, whereas this girl converses fluently and plays reciprocally at home and the silence is situational. Her selective pattern is the finding that distinguishes the two conditions. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Advise the school to require a spoken answer before she is allowed to move on to the next activity
options.rationale: Pressuring a child to speak raises anxiety at the exact moment speech is being attempted and reliably increases avoidance, which is why behavioural programs begin below the threshold at which she freezes. Communication through writing or gesture is accepted while speaking is being shaped. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Arrange repeat audiology and a speech pathology assessment before considering any psychological treatment
options.rationale: Hearing and language assessment is warranted when speech is abnormal or absent in every setting, and her hearing was formally tested last year with normal age appropriate speech documented at home. Repeating those tests delays the treatment that addresses the anxiety. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on selective mutism)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on selective mutism

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child consistently fails to speak in specific social situations, usually school, despite speaking normally in others, and it must have lasted at least one month beyond the first month of school to meet criteria. It commonly begins in early childhood in children with behavioural inhibition and a family history of anxiety, and it is frequently mislabelled as shyness, oppositionality or a language disorder. Treatment is behavioural, using graded exposure with stimulus fading, in which the child speaks first to a trusted person and gradually in the presence of others, and shaping, in which any communication is reinforced and progressively moved towards speech. School collaboration is essential because the classroom is where the avoidance lives, and pressure to speak is explicitly avoided. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, most often fluoxetine or sertraline, are added for children who do not respond to an adequate behavioural program or whose anxiety is too severe to engage with one.
key_points: The defining feature is consistent failure to speak in specific settings with normal speech in others, lasting beyond one month of school.
Normal reciprocal social communication and language at home separate it from autism and from language disorder.
Graded exposure with stimulus fading and shaping, delivered in partnership with the school, is first line.
Demanding speech increases anxiety and avoidance and is counterproductive.
Medication is reserved for severe cases or non response to an adequate behavioural program.
explanation.pearls: A short video of the child speaking freely at home, brought to the consultation by the parents, is the single most efficient way to establish that speech and language are age appropriate and to avoid an unnecessary developmental referral.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children
Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on selective mutism

subtopic_detail: Defiance and explosive tantrums at home and school in a seven year old with normal development and no aggression to others
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the mother of a seven year old boy who has had a year of daily arguments, refusal to follow instructions and tantrums lasting up to forty minutes when asked to turn off the television.

His teacher reports the same pattern at school with peers but no fighting or bullying, and his academic progress is on track. His mother says she spends most of the evening shouting and has begun to give in to stop the noise. He is well, sleeps through the night, and has no history of fire setting, cruelty to animals or stealing.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative and chatty during the consultation, normal vocabulary and comprehension for age, no motor overactivity or impulsivity observed across a twenty minute consultation, no low mood or anhedonia on direct questioning, reciprocal social interaction with normal eye contact and shared attention, growth parameters on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Teacher report scale showing elevated oppositional and defiant items with inattention and hyperactivity items in the normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence a trial of a stimulant medication and arrange review of his behaviour at home and school in four weeks
options.rationale: Stimulants treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, which frequently coexists with oppositional behaviour, but his teacher rated inattention and hyperactivity items in the normal range and no overactivity was observed. Treating the wrong target exposes him to appetite and sleep effects without addressing the behaviour. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

options.text: Refer the family to a structured parenting program that teaches consistent limits and positive reinforcement
options.rationale: Parent management training programs are the first line treatment for oppositional behaviour in primary school aged children and have the strongest evidence of any intervention, working by re-establishing predictable consequences and increasing positive attention for wanted behaviour. They also directly target the coercive cycle in which giving in to end a tantrum reinforces it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

options.text: Prescribe low dose risperidone for the tantrums and arrange metabolic monitoring at baseline and twelve weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are considered only for severe aggression that persists after an adequate psychosocial intervention, and they carry weight gain, metabolic and prolactin effects in children. Tantrums without aggression towards people or property do not meet that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer him for individual play therapy weekly and review his progress with the therapist after three months
options.rationale: Individual therapy for the child alone performs less well than parent focused intervention at this age, because the behaviour is maintained by interaction patterns at home and in the classroom. Individual work is added for older children and for comorbid anxiety or trauma. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

options.text: Arrange a paediatric review for a formal neurodevelopmental assessment before offering any behavioural intervention
options.rationale: Developmental assessment is indicated where language, learning or social communication concerns exist, and this boy has age appropriate language, on track academic progress and reciprocal social interaction. Waiting for an assessment delays an intervention that can start now. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

explanation.summary: Oppositional defiant disorder is defined by a persistent pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative and defiant behaviour and vindictiveness that exceeds what is developmentally expected and causes impairment, and it is distinguished from conduct disorder by the absence of aggression towards people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness and serious rule violation. Assessment gathers information from home and school, screens for the disorders that commonly coexist or mimic it, particularly attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, learning disorder, anxiety, depression, trauma and language disorder, and asks about parental mental health, family violence and alcohol use, all of which shape the response. Parent management training is first line and works by interrupting the coercive cycle in which escalation is rewarded by the parent withdrawing a demand. Australian programs with good evidence include group based parenting interventions delivered through community child health services. Medication has no first line role, and antipsychotics are reserved for severe persistent aggression after psychosocial treatment, with baseline and ongoing metabolic monitoring.
key_points: Oppositional defiant disorder lacks the aggression, property destruction and serious rule breaking that define conduct disorder.
Assessment requires collateral from school and screening for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, learning, mood, anxiety and trauma.
Parent management training is the first line intervention at primary school age.
Giving in to end a tantrum reinforces it, which is the specific pattern these programs target.
Antipsychotic medication is reserved for severe persistent aggression after psychosocial treatment has been tried.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the behaviour occurs with every adult or only with one: defiance confined to a single caregiver points to the interaction pattern and predicts a strong response to parent training, whereas behaviour that is identical across all settings and adults raises the likelihood of a coexisting neurodevelopmental disorder.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children
BMJ Best Practice: Oppositional defiant disorder

subtopic_detail: Discharge planning after inpatient opioid withdrawal in a man whose tolerance has fallen
stem:
You are the registrar discharging a 34 year old man from a six day inpatient withdrawal admission for heroin dependence. He has used intravenously for eight years and has had two previous non fatal overdoses.

He has declined opioid agonist treatment for now and plans to stay with his sister, who is in the room and asks what she should do if she finds him unresponsive. He says he intends to stay off heroin but acknowledges he has relapsed after previous admissions.

data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented with no withdrawal features, pupils 3 mm and equal, no track marks with surrounding cellulitis, chest clear, no oedema, gait steady
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits, hepatitis C antibody positive with undetectable viral load after treatment, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 420 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step to take before he leaves the ward?

options.text: Give him written overdose prevention information and a follow up appointment with the community drug service
options.rationale: Written information and follow up are worthwhile but neither reverses an overdose in the minutes that matter, and the first weeks after withdrawal are when the risk is highest. Information supplements the antidote rather than substituting for it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine

options.text: Arrange a naltrexone implant before discharge to block the effect of any opioid he uses in the coming months
options.rationale: Naltrexone implants are not registered or routinely funded in Australia and available depot preparations are used in limited settings with specialist oversight, and blocking treatment in someone who may resume use carries its own overdose risk when the blockade wanes. It is not the step that protects him in the first weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine

options.text: Supply take home naloxone and train both him and his sister to recognise an overdose and give it
options.rationale: Opioid tolerance falls substantially within days of abstinence, so the period immediately after withdrawal treatment or release from custody carries the highest overdose mortality, and take home naloxone supplied with training to the person and to those around them reduces deaths. In Australia naloxone is available free without a prescription through the take home naloxone program at participating pharmacies and services. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program

options.text: Prescribe a short course of diazepam to manage the anxiety and insomnia that commonly follow withdrawal treatment
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines combined with opioids are a leading contributor to fatal respiratory depression, so supplying them to a person at high risk of resuming opioid use increases the danger. Post withdrawal insomnia is managed with non drug measures and review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine

options.text: Defer naloxone supply until he has decided about opioid agonist treatment at his community appointment next week
options.rationale: Supply is not conditional on accepting agonist treatment, and the week between discharge and that appointment is precisely the window of greatest risk. Naloxone is offered to everyone at risk of witnessing or experiencing an opioid overdose. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program

explanation.summary: Loss of tolerance is the central mechanism behind overdose deaths after any period of abstinence, and the days and weeks following inpatient withdrawal, hospital discharge or release from custody carry a mortality risk many times higher than continued use. Take home naloxone addresses this directly: the Australian program supplies naloxone as a prefilled syringe or nasal spray free of charge and without a prescription to people at risk and to their family, friends and support workers. Training covers recognising overdose through unresponsiveness, slow or absent breathing and blue lips, calling for an ambulance, giving naloxone, and repeating the dose because naloxone has a shorter duration of action than most opioids. Supply is offered alongside, not instead of, the interventions with the strongest evidence for reducing mortality in opioid dependence, which are methadone and buprenorphine maintenance. Co-prescribed benzodiazepines and alcohol substantially increase overdose risk and are avoided in this population.
key_points: Tolerance falls within days of abstinence, making the post withdrawal period the highest risk window for fatal overdose.
Take home naloxone is free and prescription free in Australia and is supplied with brief training.
Training includes giving repeat doses because naloxone wears off before most opioids do.
Supply is offered regardless of whether the person accepts opioid agonist treatment.
Benzodiazepines and alcohol markedly increase the risk of fatal respiratory depression with opioids.
explanation.pearls: Naloxone has a duration of action of roughly 30 to 90 minutes while heroin lasts longer and methadone far longer, so anyone who is revived must still go to hospital and the person giving naloxone is taught to expect to repeat the dose after a few minutes if breathing does not return.

sources.label: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program

subtopic_detail: Subacute cognitive complaints with prominent self reported memory failure and poor effort on testing in a seventy four year old
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74 year old man brought by his daughter because he says his memory has gone. He can date the onset to about four months ago, shortly after his wife died, and he tells you in detail how many things he has forgotten.

He has stopped going to bowls, wakes at four in the morning and has lost 6 kg without trying. During cognitive testing he answers I do not know to most questions without attempting them, and his daughter says he manages his medications and his banking without error at home.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor slowing with reduced spontaneous speech, restricted affect, no thought disorder, no hallucinations or delusions, no tremor or rigidity, gait normal with good arm swing, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21 out of 30 with performance improving on delayed recall when cues are given
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), computed tomography of the brain reported as age appropriate atrophy with no focal lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer him to a memory clinic for amyloid positron emission tomography imaging to clarify the underlying pathology
options.rationale: Molecular imaging is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty in specialist settings after reversible contributors have been treated, and it is not funded for routine use in Australia. Performing it while an untreated depressive episode is driving the presentation risks an incorrect and irreversible diagnostic label. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor and arrange repeat cognitive testing in the practice in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are indicated once a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease or a related dementia is established, and they carry gastrointestinal and bradycardic effects. Starting one here treats a diagnosis that has not been made and leaves the depressive episode untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer him for a driving assessment and advise the licensing authority of a likely progressive cognitive disorder
options.rationale: Notification and formal driving assessment follow a diagnosis of a progressive cognitive disorder or clear evidence of unsafe driving, neither of which is established here. Acting on a provisional label has serious consequences for independence and for the therapeutic relationship. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)
source_refs: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive

options.text: Treat the depressive episode and repeat formal cognitive assessment once his mood has responded
options.rationale: A dateable subacute onset, prominent self reported memory failure, do not know responses with recall that improves on cueing, and preserved instrumental function point to cognitive impairment driven by depression, which improves as mood is treated. Repeating cognitive assessment after treatment is what separates a reversible depressive picture from a neurodegenerative one, and a proportion will still prove to have an underlying dementia. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: Reassure him that grief explains his symptoms and review him in six months to see whether they have settled
options.rationale: Bereavement is the trigger but early morning waking, six kilograms of unintentional weight loss and withdrawal from valued activities describe a depressive episode rather than uncomplicated grief. Six months of untreated depression in an older man carries substantial suicide risk. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Depression in older adults frequently presents with cognitive impairment, historically called pseudodementia, and distinguishing it from early neurodegenerative disease is one of the commonest diagnostic problems in old age psychiatry. Several features favour a depressive cause: a relatively abrupt onset that the person can date, prominent complaints about memory rather than the minimisation typical of Alzheimer disease, do not know answers rather than confabulated or near miss responses, recall that improves substantially with cueing, and preserved performance of complex instrumental tasks at home. Biological depressive features such as early morning waking, weight loss and anhedonia support the diagnosis, and a reversible medical screen and structural imaging are still performed. Treating the depression, with an antidepressant and psychological therapy and with electroconvulsive therapy where the episode is severe or psychotic, and then repeating cognitive assessment once mood has improved, is the definitive diagnostic step. Follow up remains important because a substantial proportion of older people with depression related cognitive impairment are later diagnosed with dementia, so cognitive review continues even after a good response.
key_points: Dateable subacute onset with prominent memory complaints favours depression over neurodegenerative disease.
Do not know responses and recall that improves with cueing contrast with the impaired encoding of Alzheimer disease.
Preserved instrumental function at home is strong evidence against established dementia.
Treating the depression and repeating cognitive assessment afterwards is the diagnostic manoeuvre.
A significant proportion of these patients later develop dementia, so cognitive follow up continues.
explanation.pearls: Cued recall is the discriminating bedside test: in depression related impairment the information was stored but not retrieved, so a category cue restores it, whereas in Alzheimer disease the information was never encoded and cueing does not help.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline
